desc:
Among all non-empty suffixes of s (the substrings that end at the last character), find the one that comes last in dictionary order and return the 0-based index where it starts. A string that is a proper prefix of another is smaller than it, so for example "ab" is smaller than "abc". All suffixes have different lengths and are therefore different strings, so the answer is unique.

Examples: for s = "abab" the suffixes are abab, bab, ab, b; the largest is bab, so the answer is 1. For s = "leetcode" the answer is 3: the suffix tcode starts with the largest letter t.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Comparing every pair of suffixes directly is O(n²) per comparison in the worst case, and sorting all suffixes is far too slow for strings like "aaaa...a".
Keep two candidate starts i < j and compare the suffixes character by character, remembering the length k of the common stretch.
If s[i+k] < s[j+k], then none of the starts i .. i+k can be the maximum (each is beaten by the start shifted by j - i), so jump i past them. If it is larger, jump j by k + 1. Reset k after each jump.
editorial: This is the two-candidate technique behind the minimal-rotation and Lyndon-factorization algorithms, mirrored for the maximum. Maintain candidates i < j and the number k of equal characters already seen after both. Compare s[i+k] and s[j+k].

Equal: increase k. If s[i+k] < s[j+k]: every start in i .. i+k is smaller than the start shifted by j - i, so skip them: i += k + 1; if that makes i >= j, set j = i + 1. Otherwise symmetrically skip j += k + 1. Reset k = 0. Loop while j + k < n (when the comparison reaches the end of the string the shorter suffix is smaller automatically).
Every jump advances i or j by at least k + 1 after spending k comparisons, so the total work is O(n) with O(1) extra space. Answer i.
